inside-prison:
In 2020, pandemic lockdowns cut prisons off from the outside world. In Argentina, visits stopped, and programs ended, until an exceptional court decision allowed mobile phone use in Buenos Aires’ provincial prisons.

This project follows Paola, serving a four-year sentence in Penitentiary Unit 47, and other women navigating that shift.

Phones became essential tools to maintain family ties, continue education, and sustain a sense of self beyond incarceration.

Connectivity does not remove the walls, but inside Unit 47 it reduced isolation, strengthened support networks, and opened a bridge toward life after release.
energy-paradox:
This project documents everyday life in Ijebu Igbo, a semi-urban community two hours from Lagos, seen through the perspective of an indigene.

As unreliable public power persists, solar energy and improvised charging solutions increasingly shape how people live and work. Across homes, streets, and small businesses, access to electricity determines participation in the digital world, where communication, commerce, and family ties depend on mobile devices.

The project focuses on ordinary moments shaped by the search for power: charging a phone, keeping a business running, staying connected. Rather than technology itself, the work centers the human experience of improvisation, resilience, and uncertainty in a place where connection to the wider world remains both essential and fragile.
donna:
This long-term project is a tribute to all those, like Donna, who have left everything behind to build a better future for their families. Through her journey, I explore the human cost of exile, but also the resilience it reveals—particularly the invisible threads that bind loved ones across borders. In exile, technology has become a vital lifeline. It allows Donna to remain a mother, a daughter, and a friend—despite the physical separation.

Donna, 47, comes from a remote mountain village in the Philippines. The eldest daughter of farmers, she dreamt of becoming a nurse but left her country to pay for her children’s education. Before arriving in France 13 years ago, she paid a smuggler €13,000. Since then, she has worked full-time for a wealthy Libyan family, sending every euro home. Her sacrifices bore fruit: her eldest daughter, Nicole, is now a qualified nurse. Yet, Donna has not seen her children or parents in over a decade.

Her connection to them survives thanks to smartphones, patchy Wi-Fi, and a routine of voice messages and video calls. Technology allows her to witness birthdays, send lullabies, and offer comfort after a bad school day. These moments—fleeting but essential—are the only form of presence she can offer. I have documented this intimacy from both sides: in France, where Donna works and lives in the shadows, and in the Philippines, where her voice echoes in the family home through a cracked phone screen.

The story also speaks to the broader experience of nearly 10 million overseas Filipino workers, 80% of whom are women. In France alone, nearly 50,000 Filipinas work as domestic helpers, many of them undocumented. They are part of a global chain of care that remains largely unseen, yet sustains entire economies and generations.

Through Donna’s story, I illustrate what sociologist Abdelmalek Sayad called the “double absence”—immigrants are both invisible here and missed there. But technology has carved out a third space: one of digital presence, where love, guidance, and identity still circulate. In this space, exile is not just defined by separation, but by connection.
